title: The desk cuts itself if nothing happens
body: The stocks desk still reads Risk On at 100% invested, and that is the least informative fact in this memo. Its composite score fell from +0.055 last Friday to -0.205 today, well through the -0.10 line that cuts exposure to half. The model requires three consecutive sessions beyond that line before it acts, and today was the second. The practical consequence is unusual and worth stating plainly: if SPY simply closes flat from here, the desk drops to Balanced at 50% invested on its own. Our scenario check confirms it, reporting a 50% stocks exposure for a price held at today's level over the next five sessions. There is no down-trigger to watch, because the trigger has effectively already been pulled; what we are watching for is a rescue.

That rescue is a long way off. The level that would hold the desk at 100% is SPY at $746.32, which is 8.2% above today's $689.81 close. For a model that has been fully invested since April 2025, the asymmetry here is the story: a flat tape cuts exposure, and it takes an 8% rally inside a week to avoid the cut. Should the desk go to Balanced, the flagship's weights change from SPY 35% and QQQ 25% to SPY 17.5% and QQQ 12.5%, with the Bitcoin sleeve staying at 15% and gold at 10%. Invested capital would fall from 85% to 55%, and cash would rise from 15% to 45%.

Almost none of this week's deterioration came from the economy. The macro group moved from -0.204 to -0.212 across the five sessions, which is noise. The entire -0.260 decline in the score was price-based: trend, momentum and internals. Taking today's weighted contributions, trend accounts for -0.146, internals -0.113, momentum -0.083 and macro only -0.053. The single largest positive contribution in the whole composite is the calendar group at +0.048, which is seasonality and nothing more. Strip that one favourable factor out and today's raw composite falls from -0.343 to -0.391. An investor should understand that the only meaningful thing holding this call above water is the time of year.

The volatility group did something counterintuitive that is worth owning rather than glossing over. It improved, from -0.048 to +0.035, on the day the VIX rose 86% across the week to 35.89. The model treats extreme volatility as a contrarian panic input, so a spike large enough to look like capitulation scores positively. That is a deliberate design choice and it has been profitable historically, but it means the composite is now being flattered by the same fear that is driving prices down. Read the score with that in mind.

The shape of the damage matters more than its depth, and the shape argues against a simple reading of broad risk aversion. Equal-weight SPY beat the cap-weighted index by 2.6% this week and by 4.2% over three months. Consumer staples beat SPY by 7.2% this week and by 17.3% over three months. Small caps beat SPY by 1.2%. Semiconductors lagged SPY by 10.2% this week and by 21.4% over three months. This is a concentrated de-rating of the artificial-intelligence complex with real rotation into defensives underneath it, not an indiscriminate liquidation. The honest qualification is that by a different measure breadth is now total: our crash-watch confirmation set reports zero of nine major risk assets above their 200-day average, down 89 percentage points in three months. Everything is below trend; the magnitude is wildly uneven.

Here is the observation that cuts hardest against the growth-scare narrative. Gold fell 9.1% this week and silver fell 16.2%, alongside an 8.5% fall in SPY, while the dollar rose 0.4% and the 10-year Treasury yield sat near 5%. In a genuine flight to safety gold rallies. Precious metals falling faster than equities, with the dollar firm and long yields high, is the signature of a rate and liquidity repricing rather than a hunt for shelter. The one place we do see classic risk aversion is credit, where high-yield bonds lost 2.4% against Treasuries this week and 2.5% over three months, enough to put the credit proxy in its worst historical quintile. Credit is the signal to respect here; the metals are telling you something different from what the headlines say.

This week's data release cuts against the portfolio precisely because it was good. The University of Michigan's final November consumer sentiment reading was revised up to 51.5 from a 51.0 preliminary print, with year-ahead inflation expectations falling a full point. Consumer sentiment is a stocks desk input, though the source publishes it a month in arrears, so November will not reach the model's macro group until December. The problem is the policy path. Futures put roughly a 95% probability on a Federal Reserve rate increase at the December 9 meeting, and firm data keeps it there. Our macro group sits at -0.212 against a cash gate of -0.25; the three-month bill is up 0.44 points in six months and the 10-year is up 0.81 points, both crash-watch conditions currently on. Strong economic news that keeps the Fed tightening pushes the macro group toward that gate, and it is the gate that decides whether a Balanced call becomes Risk Off at 0% invested.

The other desks are on earlier sessions and should be read as such. The Bitcoin desk, dated the November 18 close, is Balanced at 50% with Bitcoin at $63,004; its level to watch is $48,624, a further 22.8% down, which would take it to 0%. The high-beta satellite, dated the November 13 close, is Risk Off at 0% invested. On the crash watch the stocks desk remains at Warning with 6 of 10 conditions on, unchanged on the week, and all 3 of 3 confirmation signals are on. Those confirmation signals carry a caveat we repeat every time: they are candidates from a forward test, selected from 21 tested against 24 warning episodes, which is far more tests than there were events. They are unvalidated and they change no exposure.

Ahead of us, Wednesday November 25 brings PCE inflation for October, the second estimate of third-quarter GDP and the Fed's Beige Book, with markets closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and closing early Friday. The two releases that actually feed a model input are the November jobs report on December 4, which supplies the unemployment rate, and November CPI on December 10. The Fed decision on December 9 sits between them. As for the flagship itself, its live record stands at -11.08% against -9.38% for the S&P 500 since inception on October 26, across 20 sessions. That is too short to judge, and will remain too short to judge until it has 60 sessions behind it.
